query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A multi‐fidelity machine learning model that is trained on both idealized simulation data and real experimental measurements (which include the effects of processing defects and 1 wt.% oxygen) will predict the temperature‐dependent conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than traditional analytical models based on perfect crystals, especially in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy containing typical processing defects and ~1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a data‐driven multi‐fidelity machine learning model that integrates both computational (ideal lattice predictions) and experimental (defect/impurity-influenced) datasets to predict conductivity.
generation.conditions: Conductivity predictions will be performed across two separate temperature regimes: cryogenic (0–200 K) and elevated temperatures (300–1200 K), on samples similar to the characterized polycrystalline alloy with 1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence of defects and oxygen impurities (which act as scattering centers) that modify electron (or phonon) transport compared to a perfect crystal lattice.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating data from both idealized simulations and real-world measurements, the ML model learns the mapping between defect/impurity concentration and temperature to conductivity deviations from ideal behavior. It thereby compensates for the limitations of analytical models which assume defect-free conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will yield conductivity predictions with significantly lower prediction errors (i.e. a closer match to measured values) compared to conventional analytical methods. In the cryogenic regime, it should capture enhanced scattering from defects, while in the elevated temperature range it should correctly reflect the impact of both thermal vibrations and impurity scattering.
generation.baseline: Traditional analytical predictions that assume a defect-free crystalline lattice and do not account for the 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with similar defect populations and oxygen contamination levels, and its accuracy should be verified specifically within the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature ranges. Predictions may not extend reliably to samples with significantly different impurity concentrations or microstructural features.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in prediction accuracy is uncertain and will depend on the quantity and quality of the multi-fidelity training data. Moreover, non-linear defect interactions or unanticipated impurity effects might introduce additional uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with the documented polycrystalline structure and 1 wt.% oxygen. Measure the electrical (or thermal) conductivity in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes using high-precision techniques. In parallel, use the developed ML model to predict conductivity values under the same conditions. Compare predictions with both the traditional analytical model (assuming a defect-free lattice) and the experimental measurements.
measurements: Conductivity data as a function of temperature in the 0–200 K range (sensitive to defect/impurity scattering).
Conductivity data as a function of temperature in the 300–1200 K range (capturing both thermal activation and impurity effects).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the ML model does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in prediction accuracy (e.g., if its prediction error is not lower by a predefined margin compared to that of the analytical model) in one or both temperature regimes. For instance, if a held-out benchmark conductivity at 300 K measured on the oxygen-containing specimen deviates by <5% from the prediction of the perfect-crystal model or if the ML model's prediction error does not reduce the error by at least a similar margin (e.g., >10% improvement), then the hypothesis would be rejected.

For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. frame.system: Bulk high‐entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr, initially characterized as a polycrystalline sample that may contain common processing defects and a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
frame.goal: To create a predictive model that accurately forecasts transport properties (e.g., electrical or thermal conductivity) across both low (0–200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperature regimes by incorporating defect states and impurity effects, overcoming the limitations of traditional analytical methods.
frame.limitation: Existing analytical predictions assume perfect, defect‐free crystals, leading to inaccurate estimates when real defects and oxygen contamination are present. In addition, these models typically do not cover the wide temperature regimes for which experimental measurements exist.

frame.regime: Temperature-dependent behavior spanning cryogenic (0–200 K) and elevated (300–1200 K) conditions, where both defect scattering phenomena and impurity effects (e.g., from 1 wt.% oxygen) significantly influence conductivity.
